# Results — Study 866 (Flight-to-Quality Beta)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test: some
stocks are *true defensives* — they rally with long Treasuries on **risk-off** days. We
give each name a **flight-to-quality beta** (`beta_ftq` = its beta to the **TLT** daily
return, estimated only on down-SPY days) and test the two-sided prediction: high-FTQ-beta
names should earn a **lower** average return (you pay an insurance premium) yet deliver
**real crash protection**. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python
examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete
calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprint `357fd262912f` (panel
Close).*

*Run stamp: as-of 2026-06-30 · Fingerprint `357fd262912f` · 50 names × 4,147 rows · TLT+SPY conditioners.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape — cross-section | yfinance daily OHLC (`auto_adjust=True`, total-return), **50 liquid US large-caps**, 2010-01-04 → 2026-06-30, **4,147** dated rows/name |
| Real tape — conditioners | daily total-return closes for **TLT** (20+yr Treasury ETF, the flight-to-quality asset) and **SPY** (the market proxy whose down days define risk-off), same span, cached as `_cache/market_tlt_spy.parquet` |
| Universe | a fixed `UNIVERSE` of ~50 mega-caps, pulled through the **`quantlab.universe` survivorship guard** (`download_panel(..., allow_survivorship_bias=True)`), cached under this study's own `_cache/` |
| Signal | each name's **trailing-252-day flight-to-quality beta** = OLS slope of its daily return on the **TLT** return over the subset of days where **SPY < 0** (a risk-off day), known at each month-end (one execution lag) |
| Sort | each month rank the cross-section by `beta_ftq`; **long the bottom 20%** (low FTQ, cheap risky names), **short the top 20%** (high FTQ, the expensive hedges), equal-weight; earn the next month's return |
| Execution / costs | one documented lag: signal at month-end `t−1` → hold month `t`. The costed timer charges 2 legs × round-trip × one-way × NAV per month on the long-short; the short book pays 50 bps/yr borrow |
| Statistics | Newey-West (HAC, 6-lag) *t* on the monthly spread; one-sample *t*; Welch *t* on the pooled low-vs-high books; a 1,000-permutation placebo; a crash-day drawdown comparison; a 20-seed synthetic positive control |

**Survivorship — named on the Signal axis.** `UNIVERSE` is a **current-membership** list of
names that are liquid mega-caps *today*, so the magnitudes are an **upper bound** (delisted /
de-rated names are absent). A 50-mega-cap survivor panel is a conservative place to look for a
cross-sectional insurance-premium tilt.

## The headline — long-low-FTQ / short-high-FTQ spread (do the hedges under-earn?)

Monthly equal-weight bottom-20% minus top-20% FTQ-beta spread (n = **193** months, median 50
names/mo):

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| **spread (long low-FTQ − short high-FTQ)** | **+0.52 %/mo** (+6.24 %/yr) |
| Newey-West(6) *t* | **+1.36** |
| one-sample *t* | +1.25 |
| low-FTQ book / high-FTQ book | +1.79 %/mo / +1.27 %/mo (Welch *t* = +0.92) |

The **sign matches the claim** — the cheap risky (low-FTQ) names out-earned the expensive
hedges (high-FTQ) by about +6 %/yr, exactly the CAPM-of-insurance direction — but the premium
is **not statistically significant** on the conservative time-series HAC test (*t* = +1.36).
The "you pay for the hedge" penalty is at best a **weak** tilt on liquid mega-caps.

## Placebo — is the (weak) relation a lucky alignment of the sort?

Keep the FTQ sort but read each month's forward returns from a **name-permuted** cross-section
(signal → outcome link broken), 1,000 draws:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| observed spread | **+0.52 %/mo** |
| placebo mean (sd) | −0.0064 %/mo (0.2237) |
| position of observed | ≈ **+2.35 sd-units into the right tail** (right-tail p = 0.0080) |

So *cross-sectionally* the tilt is real (the low-FTQ names genuinely out-earned — not a lucky
sort, p = 0.008); it is the **time-series** significance that is weak, because the monthly
spread is volatile and the effect is thin. The two tests disagree on strength, and the desk
stamps to the conservative one.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2018-01-01)

| era | spread | NW *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| 2011 → 2018 (n=91) | +0.41 %/mo | +0.73 |
| 2018 → 2026 (n=102) | +0.61 %/mo | +1.18 |

The **sign is stable** (positive in both halves) but neither era clears |*t*| ≥ 2 — a weak,
not-robust premium, present but never significant.

## Crash protection — the *other* half of the claim (worst 5% of SPY days)

On the 203 worst SPY days (mean SPY **−2.59 %**), compare the two books' mean returns:

| book | mean return on crash days |
|---|--:|
| low-FTQ (the risky longs) | **−3.25 %/day** |
| high-FTQ (the hedges) | **−2.13 %/day** |
| **cushion (high − low)** | **+1.13 %/day** (Welch *t* = **+6.78**) |

This half of the claim is **strongly confirmed**: the FTQ-beta sort really does identify the
crash-cushioning names — on the worst market days the high-FTQ book lost **1.1 pp less** per
day than the low-FTQ book, a huge and highly significant gap (whereas across *all* days the
same difference is a negligible −0.02 %/day). **FTQ beta is a genuine risk characteristic**;
it just is not a robustly *priced* one on mega-caps.

## The timer — can you get paid the pay-for-the-hedge premium?

Charge 2 legs × round-trip × one-way × NAV per month on the long-short; short pays 50 bps/yr
borrow.

| one-way cost | gross/mo | cost/mo | net/mo | *t* (net) | Sharpe (net) | ~ann. |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **1 bp** | +0.52 % | 0.08 % | **+0.44 %** | +1.05 | 0.26 | +5.26 %/yr |
| **10 bps** | +0.52 % | 0.44 % | **+0.08 %** | +0.19 | 0.05 | +0.94 %/yr |

The premium is already insignificant **gross** (*t* = +1.36); costs and borrow then eat most of
what little is there — net +0.08 %/mo (*t* = +0.19) at a realistic 10 bps one-way. You cannot
reliably harvest the pay-for-the-hedge premium. **Mirage.**

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic seeded world (a market series, a TLT series that rallies on down-market days, and
names carrying a persistent flight-to-quality loading that — with `edge>0` — depresses their
forward mean). No network.

| world | spread NW *t* |
|---|--:|
| null (`edge = 0`), **20 seeds** | mean **+0.28** (sd 1.11), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 1/20 seeds** |
| planted (`edge = 0.004`, seed 866) | **+12.39** (Welch *t* = +7.70) |

The detector recovers a *planted* pay-for-the-hedge relation cleanly and stays essentially
silent on the null (one 5%-level false positive in 20 — as expected) — so the weak real-tape
result is an honest read of the tape, not a biased engine. *(A faithful-engine / power check
only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The pay-for-the-hedge premium (long low-FTQ / short high-FTQ) is
  **+0.52 %/mo** (+6.2 %/yr) with the **right sign** — the cheap risky names out-earned the
  expensive hedges — and a 1,000-permutation placebo puts it ≈+2.35 sd-units into the right
  tail (p = 0.008), so cross-sectionally it is real, not a lucky sort. But the conservative
  Newey-West *t* is only **+1.36** (one-sample +1.25), it fails |*t*| ≥ 2, and neither era
  clears significance (+0.73 / +1.18). The *crash-protection* half of the claim, by contrast,
  is **strongly confirmed** (high-FTQ book cushions the worst SPY days by +1.13 %/day, Welch
  *t* = +6.78): FTQ beta is a genuine risk characteristic, just not a robustly priced one on
  mega-caps. *Survivorship: current-membership mega-caps — magnitudes are an upper bound.*
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The premium is insignificant even gross; at 1 bp one-way net
  +0.44 %/mo (*t* = +1.05) and at 10 bps net +0.08 %/mo (*t* = +0.19) — costs plus borrow eat
  it and it never clears significance. You get the crash hedge; the market does not reliably pay
  you a harvestable premium for holding the other side.
- **Crash-protection (descriptive) — CONFIRMED.** The sort does what it says on the tin: the
  high-FTQ book really cushions crashes (+1.13 %/day on the worst 5% of SPY days, *t* = +6.78).
  A risk-management fact, not a return edge — reported as a third, informational axis.
